title: Angles Around a Point Theorem
summary: Consecutive angles around a point that fill a full turn add to 360°. This is also commonly called the angles at a point theorem.
proofIdea: Choose one boundary ray and add its opposite ray through the common vertex. On each side of the resulting line, use a Protractor coordinate system to order the boundary rays from 0° to 180°. The consecutive angle sizes are successive coordinate differences, so their sum telescopes to 180° on each side. The two half-plane sums therefore total 360°. If the added opposite ray splits an original angle, put that angle's first side at 0° on its own Protractor scale. If the new ray and the other side have coordinates x° and y°, the two pieces have sizes x° and (y − x)°, which add to the original size y°. Thus the auxiliary ray does not change the original full-turn sum.
explorationPrompt: Choose three, four, or five angles, move their boundary rays, and compare the changing angles with the 360° total.

proofSteps.title: Set the two degree scales
proofSteps.detail: Choose one boundary ray OA and add its opposite ray OX. In the half-plane on one side of line AX, use OA as coordinate 0° and OX as 180°. In the other half-plane, use OX as coordinate 0° and OA as 180°.

proofSteps.title: Telescope the first half-plane
proofSteps.detail: List the ray coordinates in the first half-plane as 0 = a₀ < a₁ < ··· < aₖ = 180. The consecutive angle sizes are a₁ − a₀, a₂ − a₁, and so on. Adding them cancels every interior coordinate and leaves aₖ − a₀ = 180°.

proofSteps.title: Telescope the second half-plane
proofSteps.detail: Apply the same Protractor-coordinate argument in the other half-plane. Its successive coordinate differences also telescope from 0° to 180°, so the consecutive angles there total 180°.

proofSteps.title: Recover the original full turn
proofSteps.detail: The two half-plane sums cover the full turn without overlap, so together they give 180° + 180° = 360°. If OX split an original angle, use a Protractor scale with the first original side at 0°, OX at x°, and the other side at y°. The pieces x° and (y − x)° add to the original size y°, so removing OX does not change the total.
